prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’ve lived within half a mile of it for twenty years. West by the black iron weather-hen half-strangled with clematis on the garage roof I can locate it. Past a low ridge in the cliff face of a limestone dale there’s a cave in the bushes. When the old tigers were long since gone, leaving their teeth, the valley people would climb there with the dead they thought most useful; push them well in, take them out again, walk them around: ‘They’re coming! They’re coming’ We Malagasies love our second burials. We hire a band that comes in a van. Again with liquefaction almost done we hold our cherished ones in our arms. From the grave-clothes they fall in gobbets as dog-food falls from the can. We wrap them in fresh dry linen. They bless our lives with their happiness. Walk them around the valley. Drop here a finger for the god that is a rat or a raven, here a metatarsal to set under the hearth for luck. And what was luck? The afterlife back then was fairly long: nothing demented like for ever, nothing military. The afterlife would come to the party.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: West, Past, When

outputs.L1:
I’ve lived within half a mile of it for twenty years. I can locate it to the west, by the black iron weather-hen on the garage roof, half-strangled by clematis. Beyond a low ridge in the cliff face of a limestone dale, there is a cave among the bushes. Long after the old tigers had vanished, leaving only their teeth, the valley people would climb up with the dead they considered most useful. They would push them deep inside, bring them out again, and walk them around: ‘They’re coming! They’re coming!’

We Malagasies love our second burials. We hire a band that arrives in a van. Once liquefaction is nearly complete, we hold our cherished ones in our arms again. They fall from their grave-clothes in gobbets, as dog food falls from a can. We wrap them in fresh, dry linen. With their happiness, they bless our lives. We walk them around the valley, dropping here a finger for the god that is a rat or a raven, there a metatarsal to place beneath the hearth for luck.

And what was luck? The afterlife, back then, was fairly long: nothing demented like forever, nothing military. The afterlife would come to the party.
outputs.L2:
For two decades, my home has stood less than half a mile away. I can pinpoint the place by looking west beyond the garage roof, where clematis nearly chokes the black iron weather vane shaped like a hen. Beyond a shallow ledge in the limestone valley’s cliff, a cave lies hidden among shrubs.

Long after the ancient tigers had disappeared, leaving only their teeth behind, the valley’s inhabitants carried up the bodies of those they considered most valuable. They shoved the dead deep into the cave, brought them back out, and paraded them around, crying, “They’re on their way! They’re on their way!”

We Malagasy people cherish our reburial ceremonies. A hired band arrives by van. When decomposition has almost reduced our loved ones to liquid, we cradle them once more. Chunks spill from their burial garments like canned dog food sliding from its tin. We dress the remains in clean, dry linen, and their joy bestows blessings upon us. Then we carry them in procession through the valley. A finger may be left for a deity embodied as a rat or raven; a metatarsal may be placed beneath the hearth to bring good fortune.

But what did good fortune mean? In those days, existence after death lasted a reasonably long time—never anything absurd like eternity, and nothing regimented or martial. The dead would return to join the celebration.
outputs.L3:
For twenty years, the narrator has lived near a hidden cave in a limestone valley. Once inhabited by tigers, the cave later became a sacred place where local people performed rituals involving the remains of their valued dead. These practices reflect Malagasy second-burial traditions, in which families exhume their loved ones, hold their decomposing remains, and wrap them carefully in fresh linen.

The dead are then carried in procession around the valley, allowing them to rejoin the community in a symbolic celebration. Afterward, their bones may be left in the cave as offerings or kept as charms believed to bring good luck. Through these customs, the passage presents the afterlife not as eternal or frightening, but as finite and peaceful. Death does not entirely separate people from their community; the dead remain capable of participating in shared rituals, celebrations, and the continuing life of the valley.
outputs.L4:
A nearby cave invites speculation about how ancient communities may have cared for their dead. Its darkness, narrow passages, and hidden chambers suggest more than a place of disposal: perhaps bodies were carried there in solemn procession, laid out for a time, and later revisited. In such a setting, burial would not have marked an abrupt separation between the living and the dead. The cave could instead have served as a threshold where bodies changed gradually and where relatives returned to gather, rearrange, or transport their remains.

Malagasy secondary-burial traditions offer a vivid way of imagining this continuing relationship. In practices such as *famadihana*, the dead may be removed from family tombs, wrapped in fresh cloth, lifted onto shoulders, and carried among their descendants. The occasion combines reverence with movement, music, conversation, feasting, and celebration. Ancestors are not treated as distant abstractions. Their remains possess weight and texture; they can be touched, held, dressed, and brought back into the social world.

These rituals also redistribute the dead. Bones may be gathered together, separated, rewrapped, or placed among other relatives, allowing kinship to be expressed through the arrangement of physical remains. A person’s social existence therefore continues after biological death. The ancestor remains involved in family identity, memory, inheritance, and collective fortune. Proper care for the dead may invite protection and good luck, while neglect may threaten the well-being of the living.

Seen in this light, the ancient cave and the Malagasy tomb represent related ways of refusing to make death an immediate, final disappearance. The afterlife is finite and intimate rather than infinitely remote. It unfolds through the body’s transformation and through repeated acts of human attention. By carrying and rearranging the dead, communities make loss manageable and preserve bonds across generations. Mourning becomes inseparable from reunion, and burial becomes not a single ending but an ongoing communal practice in which ancestors remain present through touch, memory, obligation, and celebration.
outputs.L5:
### When the West Was Past

When the sun slipped into the West, the road turned gold behind us. We did not look back. The past had followed us long enough—through empty towns, over silent hills, and across rivers that remembered every name we tried to forget.

Ahead, night gathered on the horizon. We did not know what waited there, only that it was new.

And sometimes, new was reason enough to keep going.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a hidden limestone cave, prehistoric burial customs, and Madagascar’s tradition of second burial, blending archaeology with intimate personal memory.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Cave Remembers in Layers**

The cave opened beneath the hill like a held breath. Limestone, rain-eaten and pale, folded us into its mineral dark. Our lamps moved over curtains of calcite, over stalagmites rising like blunt candles, over the small, deliberate silences left by the dead. In a chamber narrowed by centuries, we found the burial: knees drawn toward the ribs, hands near the face, red ochre gathered in the hollows of bone. A pierced shell lay beside the skull, though the sea was many days away.

Someone had carried it here.

That fact entered me more deeply than any date. Before pottery, before iron, before names could be kept in ink, someone crossed a long country with a shell in the palm, believing the dead should not enter darkness empty-handed.

I thought of my grandmother’s dresser, its shallow drawer fragrant with camphor and dust. After she died, I opened it and found the comb still holding three silver hairs. I wrapped them in a handkerchief and carried them home, ashamed of the theft, comforted by its weight. Archaeology teaches us to label such things—grave good, pigment, secondary deposit—but love resists the clean edge of a tag. Love says: this was touched. This was chosen. This crossed a distance.

In Madagascar, among some peoples of the highlands, the dead may be welcomed again through *famadihana*, the turning of the bones. Years after burial, families open the tomb, lift their ancestors into daylight, wrap them in fresh silk, speak their names, dance with them beneath the living sky. It is not resurrection. It is not farewell repeated. It is kinship refusing to become past tense.

I imagine the cloth bright against the plateau, music shaking dust from the road, hands careful around the small architecture of a shoulder. The dead return altered, yet intimate; the living return altered too. Each embrace says the body is not merely what remains, but what memory continues to carry.

In the cave, we worked with brushes finer than eyelashes. Grain by grain, the earth surrendered a wrist, a tooth, the faint crescent of a child’s rib. Above us, water wrote its slow white script. Every drop added something to the stone; every touch risked taking something away.

My father once lifted me across a flooded ditch. I remember his shirt smelling of rain and engine oil, his wrist under my knees. Years later, when illness made him light, I lifted him from bed to chair. His bones seemed already to know another gravity. Neither of us spoke of the reversal. Outside, rain tapped the windows with the patience of caves.

Perhaps burial has always been this: a grammar for carrying what can no longer carry itself.

The prehistoric mourners entered with fire. They passed beneath the low limestone lip, bearing the folded body, the ochre, the impossible shell. Perhaps they sang. Perhaps they were silent from fear. Perhaps one person, walking last, touched the wall to remember the way out. Their hand left no print, yet I feel it there whenever my lamp crosses the stone—a warmth imagined across ten thousand years.

We close the excavation at dusk. The bones are covered, the measurements checked, the cave returned to darkness. Still, the dead travel with us. They cling to our notebooks, our cuffs, the chambers behind our ribs.

And I think of the silk being unfolded in Madagascar, of ancestors lifted once more into weather; of my grandmother’s hairs in their square of cloth; of my father’s arm, first strong beneath me, then fragile in mine. The earth receives us, but never only once. We are buried in soil, in stone, in the gestures of those who loved us. We are exhumed by music, by objects, by a remembered scent opening suddenly in a room.

Deep under the hill, limestone gathers around an ancient absence, making it luminous.

Someone carried a shell into the dark.

Someone is carrying it still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a narrator who has lived near an ancient cave for twenty years and begins describing how early valley people carried their dead in and out of it. Let the narration drift surreally into a Malagasy famadihana ceremony and reflections on the afterlife.
counterfactuals.output:
For twenty years I have lived within sight of the cave.

In winter its mouth is black. In summer, when the valley whitens under heat, it exhales a mineral coolness that reaches my garden by evening. I have found moths resting on my door that seemed powdered with its darkness.

The first people here carried their dead up the slope on litters of hazel and hide. I imagine their feet slipping in the chalk, their shoulders bent beneath the beloved weight. They entered singing—or perhaps they entered without sound. They laid the bodies in the inner chambers among beads, blades, antler pins, bowls of grain. Later they returned. They gathered what remained, wrapped it, moved it deeper. Sometimes they carried the bones back into daylight.

Thus the dead traveled in and out of the hill.

I think of them descending through rain, an ancestor between them, clean and pale as winter wood. Perhaps a child touched the skull and was told: This is your mother’s mother. Perhaps no one explained. The valley itself was explanation enough: mist rising from the river, cattle lowing behind thorn fences, smoke lying flat over the roofs.

After twenty years, I no longer believe the cave is empty.

At night it lengthens. Its passages run beneath the sea and come up, impossibly, in Madagascar, where the tombs open under a lucid sky. Music approaches—trumpets, drums, voices bright with reunion. The dead are lifted out in their old wrappings. Families unfold new silk, lay the ancestors upon it, turn them gently, speak their names. Dust dances in the sun.

Then the valley people are there too, though they have crossed thousands of years without surprise. They bring their bone bundles from the cave. The Malagasy families make room. Someone laughs. Someone pours rum upon the ground. The musicians play faster.

The dead, wrapped anew, are carried on shoulders and danced around the tomb.

I watch from the cave mouth, or from my garden, or from the narrow country between sleep and waking. The two landscapes pass through each other: red earth beneath chalk hills, rice fields shining where the river meadow should be, zebu horns moving among the yews. Silk shrouds stream like banners. Ancient finger bones knock softly together in woven bags.

What is an afterlife, if not this repeated lifting?

Not a kingdom beyond the stars, perhaps. Not judgment, not oblivion. Perhaps it is simply the stubborn refusal of the living to leave the dead in one place. We carry them inward, carry them outward. We wrap them in hide, in silk, in memory. We give them darkness until we miss their faces, then bring them into the sun.

By morning the music is gone. The cave stands across the valley, sealed in blue shadow.

Still, some evenings, the wind arrives smelling of dust and rice straw. I hear footsteps climbing the old path, many feet keeping time, and I know that inside the hill the dead are being turned again—not away from us, but toward us, so they may continue their long, patient looking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, visceral piece of literary prose in which bones, weathered landmarks, animal gods, grave-clothes, luck, and communal celebrations of the dead are woven together in a single flowing monologue.
counterfactuals.output:
By autumn the hills had given up their bones. Ribs of cattle shone among the thistles; finger-bones worked loose from the old cemetery wall and clicked downhill in the rain, pale dice thrown by a hand too large to see. We gathered them without asking whose they were. In our village, the dead belonged to everyone, the way weather did, the way hunger did. We washed each little relic in vinegar and laid it beneath the weathered milestone at the crossroads, where the carved numbers had been erased by a century of hands and storms, and where the stone saint had lost his face to frost. There we asked for luck, though luck had always been a black dog nosing at the door, eager to enter, eager to bite. We tied red thread around the saint’s broken wrists. We tucked coins into the cracks. We told ourselves the road remembered where it led.

Above us, clouds came down like grave-clothes stripped from giants. They snagged on the bell tower and trailed their hems through the fields; by dusk the whole valley smelled of wet wool, extinguished candles, and earth newly opened. That was when the animal gods returned. The antlered one stood between the birches, his eyes full of distant fires. The sow-goddess rooted beneath the gallows hill, turning up teeth and wedding rings. In the river, the eel-father wound himself around the drowned bridge piers and whispered the names of those who had crossed in winter and not come home. No one bowed. No one needed to. We had carried these gods in our blood so long that worship was only another word for fear endured together.

On the Night of Lanterns we dressed the dead in their grave-clothes again—not the true dead, not their stubborn bodies folded under stone, but their remembered shapes. We stuffed shirts with straw, pinned veils to broom handles, painted familiar mouths on sacks of flour. Here was Grandmother Ysra with her crooked jaw; here the miller who laughed during the flood; here the six children taken by fever, each given a crown of rowan berries and a candle no wind could seem to kill. We set them at the long tables among us. We poured them wine. We pushed the fattest portions of meat toward their empty sleeves. Then the fiddles began, thin and furious, and the drums answered from the barns, and every living heel struck the ground as if demanding entrance to the country below.

We danced until mud climbed our calves and rain slicked our faces like oil. We kissed skulls polished smooth by generations of palms. We wore vertebrae on cords and shook knucklebones in cups, casting fortunes across the feast boards: a six for marriage, a one for blood, a blank bone for the silence beyond all prediction. When my turn came, the bones rolled beneath the lantern light and stopped in a pattern no elder would name. Around me the village roared, drunk on grief, drunk on survival. Someone crowned the faceless saint with ivy. Someone led the straw children through the square. Someone opened the cemetery gate, and whether it was the wind that moved among us afterward, lifting hems and touching shoulders, or whether the dead had truly risen in their patient grave-clothes, no one dared spoil the celebration by asking.

I felt my mother near me then, though we had buried her in spring beneath a sky white as an animal’s belly. I felt the old pressure of her hand at the back of my neck. Dance, it said. Dance while the bones still obey you. So I danced past the milestone, past the ruined watchtower, past the well whose stones had been worn hollow by the ropes of vanished hands. The antlered god paced me in the dark. The sow-goddess grunted beneath the music. Overhead the grave-clouds tore open, and cold stars glittered like nails driven through the night.

At dawn we carried the effigies to the hill and burned them. Their painted faces blackened; their straw lungs filled with flame. We sang louder than the crackling, louder than the crows. Ash settled on our hair, our tongues, our wedding rings. The children chased it laughing, believing each flake a blessing, each ember a soul choosing its next house. Perhaps they were right. Perhaps luck is nothing but the dead walking close enough to warm us, close enough to steer our feet around the open grave. Perhaps every road sign, every broken shrine, every bone whitening in the ditch is an instruction written in a language the body understands.

When the fire sank, we went home beneath a clean, merciless sky, leaving the hill to smoke and the gods to feed. Behind us, under ash and trampled flowers, the scattered bones lay quiet. But not silent. Never silent. In their small white chambers, the whole village went on singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental first-person meditation that connects a barely visible cave in an English limestone dale with prehistoric excarnation and modern Malagasy reburial rites. Use precise, unsettling physical imagery and end with the idea that the afterlife joins the party.
counterfactuals.output:
The cave is not a mouth until I know it is there.

Before that: a bruise in the limestone, half-screened by hart’s-tongue fern, where the dale folds its grey knees together. Sheep pass above it without looking down. Rain combs the scree. The entrance is scarcely wider than my shoulders and has the colour of old teeth.

I kneel. The ground exhales calcium, leaf rot, the cold mineral breath of water that has never seen weather. Inside, my torch finds a rib of rock, a puddle skinned with ochre, a harvestman balancing on its hair-thin legs. The beam does not illuminate the darkness so much as push a small dent into it.

People came here before there was a word for England.

Perhaps they brought bones.

Perhaps they brought bodies and waited.

I imagine—not history, but an ache arranged like history—the dead laid out on a limestone shelf above the valley. Tendons tightening into cords. Lips shrinking from teeth. The abdomen loosening first, then the weather entering: bluebottles, rain, the precise beaks of crows. A fox worrying the small bones of a hand apart as delicately as someone unfastening hooks.

Excarnation: the word sounds clean, almost clerical. The fact would have been wet. Skin becoming parchment, then ribbon. A kneecap rolling in grass. Vertebrae exposed one by one, pale counters threaded briefly on the dark string of the spine.

Later, someone gathers what remains.

Not everything. Never everything.

A femur still greasy at the head. A jaw with soil in its sockets. Teeth clicking in a woven bag as the bearer descends towards this almost-invisible fissure. I crawl farther in and feel the roof graze my back. Limestone powder whitens my coat. The cave accepts me by abrasion.

What was a person when carried here?

Not the face, gone. Not the voice. Weight, perhaps. Arrangement. The stubborn architecture beneath resemblance.

I think of Madagascar, though the distance is absurd: this wet dale, those highland tombs; this solitary torch, the music and bright cloth of famadihana. In some Malagasy communities, at intervals determined by family, means, omen, and obligation, ancestors are brought again into daylight. The tomb is opened. The dead, wrapped in old shrouds, are lifted and rewrapped in fresh silk or cloth. Families speak to them. Musicians play. People dance with the bundled ancestors held close—not corpses returned to life, not relics in a museum, but kin whose place in the family requires touch, expense, laughter, renewal.

I picture the cloth darkened where old matter has seeped into it. The bundle’s unexpected lightness. A corner giving beneath the hand because what felt like a shoulder has become separate pieces. Dust at the knot. Perfume, sweat, stone, decomposition’s last dry sweetness.

To disturb the dead: in one language, desecration. In another circumstance, care.

Here in the cave, I cannot stand. My thighs tremble. Water counts seconds into a pool. I wonder whether the prehistoric dead were hidden from sight or made visible in stages—first offered to weather, then sorted, then carried underground. Whether grief needed sequence: flesh, bone, darkness. Whether the mourners touched the skull one final time, thumbs resting in the smooth hollows behind the ears.

We like burial to be a door.

But these rites make it a hinge.

The dead pass out of the social world and are carried back into it. They weather, travel, change clothes. They become lighter and more numerous. They lose their faces yet accumulate names. The living bend around them like dancers adjusting to a difficult partner.

When I reverse from the cave, limestone scraping my spine, daylight arrives ankle-first. The dale is offensively green. A ewe tears grass with square yellow teeth. My palms are furred with mud and fine white powder, as if I have handled something ground down beyond recognition.

Behind me, the entrance disappears again.

I think of bones waiting in the hill, of bright new shrouds circling old fragments, of music crossing the point where language fails. We do not leave the dead behind. We revise the choreography, widen the circle, make room among the breathing.

And then the afterlife joins the party.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose-poem about people maintaining affectionate, practical relationships with their ancestors: carrying corpses around a valley, rewrapping decomposing relatives, distributing bones for luck, and imagining an afterlife that is temporary, joyful, and neither eternal nor militarized.
counterfactuals.output:
Each morning we carry our dead around the valley so they will not forget the turns: the river’s silver elbow, the fig tree split by weather, the path where goats insist upon being wiser than men. They ride on our shoulders, lightened by time, wrapped in cloth bright enough to embarrass the sun. We tell them who married, who returned, which roof leaks. Affection is practical here. It has knots, handles, a schedule.

When the wrappings loosen and the beloved body begins its patient undoing, we wash what can be washed, oil what can be oiled, and wind the cloth again. No one pretends the sweet rot is not rot. No one mistakes decay for departure. An aunt’s finger bone goes to the baker for luck with rising dough; a grandfather’s rib rests above a doorway; a small white knuckle is sewn into a traveler’s pocket so the road will recognize kin. Thus the dead are distributed among necessary things: bread, thresholds, journeys, rain.

We do not imagine eternity. Eternity would be rude, a guest who never leaves. Beyond us is only a festival of reasonable length: music, shade, ripe fruit, the recovered voices of those who died too young. There are no battlements, no trumpets ordering souls into lines, no captains, no victorious banners. The dead dance without rank. They drink until their grief grows drowsy. Then, when joy has finished its work, they loosen like mist from the valley and enter whatever comes after afterlife—perhaps soil, perhaps weather, perhaps nothing we need to name.

Until then, we carry them. Until then, they carry us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
